blocks.text: Alkhabeer Diversified Income Traded Fund (“the Fund”) is a closed-ended Shari’a-compliant investment traded fund established in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and regulated by the Capital Market Authority (CMA). The Fund’s investment objective is to generate periodic income to investors by investing in Shari’a-compliant income generating assets. The Fund Manager “Alkhabeer Capital” plans to invest in Sukuk, trade finance transactions, leasing transactions, income funds and Murabaha transactions, either directly or through investment funds.

4. Standard Deviation is a measure of risk. It is calculated as any volatility in returns over a period of time. The lower the volatility, the more homogeneous the set of returns.
5. Sharpe Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the difference as the Fund Manager excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by the Standard Deviation. The greater a portfolio's Sharpe Ratio, the better its risk-adjusted performance.
6. Tracking Error is a measure of risks. It is calculated as the Standard Deviation between the Fund Manager's return and the Benchmark's return. The lower the Tracking Error, the lower the Fund Manager deviates from the Benchmark.
7. Beta is a measure of the average historical sensitivity of the Fund's returns compared to market returns. It is calculated by using the covariance of the Fund and the market on the variance of the market.
8. Alpha measures any excess return achieved by the Fund compared to the performance of the index.
9. Information Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the active return of the Fund Manager, divided by its tracking error. The higher the Information ratio, the higher the Fund Manager ability to generate excess returns per Unit of excess risk. Knowing that the performance and risk parameters were calculated based on the Unit's trading prices in the market.

OVERVIEW OF THE LEASING, TRADE FINANCE AND SUKUK INDUSTRIES

items: According to the December 2022 Monthly Confidence Index for the Equipment Finance Industry released by the Equipment Leasing and Finance Foundation (MCI-EFI), the overall confidence index in the equipment finance industry increased to 45.9, compared to 43.7 in November. Survey results show that 55.6% of respondents believe that business conditions will remain unchanged in the coming four months, compared to 46.4% in the previous month, while 40.7% believe that business conditions will worsen, a decrease from 53.6% in November.

The Monthly Leasing and Finance Index (MLFI-25) released by the Equipment Leasing and Finance Association (ELFA), which tracks the economic activity of 25 companies across the equipment finance sector, with a value of US$ 1 trillion, revealed that the volume of new business in November totaled US$ 8.6 billion, an increase of 9% on an annualized basis, compared to the volume of new business in November 2021. The cumulative volume of new business increased to date by 6% compared to 2021.

According to ELFA, the expansion of investments in hardware and software boomed in the second half of 2022, forming a strong launch pad into 2023, which is expected to be a year of greater difficulty for the economy and industry. In the meantime, investment in hardware and software increased by 12% (on an annualized basis) in Q3 of 2022, a significant recovery following its weak growth in Q2.
The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) stated that the volume of trade has increased in 2022, which is a sign of strong global demand.

According to the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the gap in the global trade finance transactions has continued to be wide for at least ten years. It is estimated to have grown to US$ 1.7 trillion in 2020, compared to US$ 1.5 trillion in 2018. The ADB forecasts that the gap in trade finance transactions will increase to at least US$ 2 trillion in 2022.

The significant growth in trade finance transactions is mainly attributed to the greater demand on energy products trade finance transactions. World trade is expected to reach a new high of US$ 32 million in 2022, an increase of 12% on an annualized basis, amid elastic demand on commodities and services.

According to Fitch Credit Ratings, total Sukuk issues in major markets decreased by 14.4% in Q3 of 2022. Nevertheless, outstanding global Sukuk increased by 2.1% on a quarterly basis, to reach US$ 749.6 billion.

Fitch Credit Ratings expects the activity in the Sukuk market to be slow in the short term in the key markets of the GCC, Malaysia and Indonesia due to continued volatility, higher interest rates, higher global energy prices, geopolitical events and lower demand on emerging market debts.

In spite of higher profitability, domestic issuers are expected to continue to give priority to their liquidity needs for the coming year by focusing on increasing equity through debt issuance, particularly Sukuk. According to KPMG, domestic issues in the first nine months of 2022 totaled US$ 3.8 billion. This figure is expected to increase in the coming months with banks catering to the increasing demand in the public and private sectors.

In terms of performance, losses in global Sukuk markets in 2022 are expected to mark the worst year in decades. The Sukuk market declined significantly in 2022, with Dow Jones Sukuk Index registering a decrease of 7.81%.
